To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there is a clear difference in perception of CSR activities between managers and shop floor workers in family-run businesses in Eastern Thailand, which are not reflected in the formalised CSR practices.

1) there is a strong appreciation of the informal CSR activities in FRBs with interesting gradients across different sectors, organisational hierarchy levels, gender and age group, 2) the appreciation of informal CSR activities is not evenly distributed among employees in FRBs, and 3) the appreciation of CSR activities is higher in middle management level than in shop-floor level.
• There are different levels of appreciation for intrinsic CSR activities across sectors and organisational hierarches.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the perception of CSR activities by employees in family run business (FRB), and how these perceptions differ between employees in different sectors, different organisational hierarchy levels, gender and age group.
understanding the CSR practices and perceptions of employees in family run businesses in Eastern Thailand.
the following questions: • What are the perceptions of CSR activities in FRBs and how do they differ across different organisational hierarchal levels?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the perception of CSR is different across the organisation, and this difference can be explained by the level of understanding of the CSR activities, the level of involvement of the CSR activities in the company and the strategic intent of CSR activities.
the CSR activities of the FRBs are not well known and understood by the employees and that there are differences between employees in different organisational hierarchic levels.

(1) the majority of FRBs in Thailand do have some form of CSR activities; (2) there are significant differences in perception of CSR activities between different groups in the same organisation; (3) there are significant variations in CSR activities across different FRBs; and (4) there are significant relationships between the CSR perception of employees and their organisational hierarchy, gender and age group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more CSR activities are perceived as being implemented by the company, the higher the appreciation of the employees and the more likely they would stay with the company.
CSR is an important tool for family businesses to improve the quality of their work environment and the motivation of employees.

we found that there is a strong appreciation of CSR activities among Thai employees, with interesting gradients across different sectors, organisational hierarchy, gender, age group and company sizes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CSR activities can be perceived differently by the different levels of employees in a family-run business.
there are significant differences between managers and shop-floor workers in family-run businesses in Eastern Thailand in terms of CSR activities and their perception.
CSR is not just about the big companies, it is also important in small family run businesses.
